title: What Do You Do When Your High Performer Has a Bad Attitude?
excerpt: A case study about one of the hardest situations for a manager: when someone delivers exceptional results but their behaviour is damaging the team. How do you balance performance with the way someone treats the people around them?
content:
Imagine you've got someone on your team who is absolutely brilliant at their job.

They consistently deliver. Their numbers are better than everyone else's. They solve difficult problems and hit deadlines. Senior leadership knows who they are, and whenever something important needs doing, they're one of the first people you think of. On paper, they're your star performer.

The problem is that they're also difficult to work with.

They dismiss other people's ideas. They can be unnecessarily blunt, and they don't seem very interested in how their behaviour affects the people around them. Maybe they've made someone feel stupid in a meeting. Maybe they constantly challenge colleagues in a way that feels more like criticism than collaboration. Perhaps people have started avoiding them altogether.

As their manager, you're now in a difficult position. What do you do when someone is producing exceptional results but their behaviour is making the team worse? I think this is a situation where managers can very easily fall into a trap.

## "Yes, but they're brilliant..."

I've heard variations of this argument many times:

*"Yes, they're difficult, but they're brilliant."*

*"Yes, they can be a bit of a nightmare, but look at what they deliver."*

*"We can't afford to lose them."*

I understand why managers think this way. Losing a high performer feels like a significant risk. You know exactly what that person delivers, and you probably don't have someone waiting to step in and produce the same results tomorrow. So it's tempting to tolerate a bit of bad behaviour in exchange for the output.

But you're not getting that output for free. You're paying for it somewhere else. Other people may be spending time dealing with the difficult person. Quieter team members may stop contributing because they don't want to be dismissed. Collaboration may start to break down, and someone who would otherwise have stayed may eventually decide they've had enough and leave. Once you count all that, the person who looked like your best performer may not be adding as much as their individual numbers suggest.

## Performance isn't just about the numbers

This is something I've changed my thinking on over the years. Being a high performer is about what you produce and also about how you produce it.

Someone who delivers 20% more than everyone else but makes three other people significantly less effective isn't the outstanding performer their numbers suggest. Someone who consistently gets great results while making the people around them better is providing a very different kind of value.

That matters even more as people become more senior. The more experienced someone is, the more their impact extends beyond their own work. They influence other people, set standards and shape the culture around them. People watch how they behave, especially if they're seen as successful.

That's why I think managers need to be careful about treating "performance" and "behaviour" as if they're independent. The way someone behaves is part of their performance.

## What you tolerate becomes the standard

This is probably the most important part of the whole situation.

Imagine you're one of the other people on that team. You watch someone repeatedly dismiss colleagues, behave badly in meetings and create tension, and you notice that nothing really happens because they're very good at their job.

You probably don't conclude that your manager has made a nuanced decision about balancing performance against behavioural concerns. You think, *"Apparently, that's acceptable if you're good enough."*

The message doesn't just go to the person behaving badly. It goes to everyone, and it tells them what the organisation really values. You can talk about respect, collaboration and psychological safety as much as you like, but people pay far more attention to what happens than to what's written in a company values document.

That's why I really like this phrase: "What you tolerate teaches everybody else what actually matters around here."

If you keep excusing poor behaviour because someone delivers good results, you've made a decision about what matters. You've decided that results are more important than the way people are treated.

## So what do you actually do?

I wouldn't immediately put someone on a performance plan or start looking for a way to get rid of them. If they really are a high performer, I'd want to keep them. But I'd also want to address the behaviour, and do it directly.

One approach I've found useful is to think about feedback in three parts: What, So What, Now What. It's simple, but it gives you somewhere to start.

### What

Start by describing the behaviour. Leave out their personality, your interpretation of their intentions, and anything like *"You have a bad attitude."* Be specific:

*"In yesterday's meeting, when Sarah suggested a different approach, you interrupted her and told her the idea didn't make sense before she'd finished explaining it."*

You're describing something that happened. That matters because vague feedback is very hard to act on. If you tell someone they're "negative" or have a "bad attitude", they can reasonably ask what that means. Specific behaviour gives them something they can recognise and change.

### So What

Then explain the impact:

*"The problem isn't that you disagreed with Sarah. I actually want you to challenge ideas. The problem is that the way you responded shut the conversation down, and I've noticed people are becoming less willing to contribute when you're in the room."*

You're connecting the behaviour to its consequences, and this is where I think managers sometimes miss something important: you don't need to prove bad intentions. They might have been trying to help. They might not have realised how they came across, or they might think they're just being direct. Their intention doesn't change the impact. You can accept that someone didn't mean to cause a problem while being very clear that their behaviour is causing one.

### Now What

Finally, explain what needs to happen differently:

*"I need you to challenge ideas, because your experience is valuable, but I need you to do it in a way that lets other people contribute. Let people finish. Ask questions before dismissing an idea. If you disagree, explain why instead of shutting the conversation down."*

This is the bit that turns feedback into something useful. As well as telling someone what's wrong, you're giving them a clear picture of what good looks like.

## The conversation might be uncomfortable

There's no getting around it. A conversation like this can be difficult, particularly if the person has been praised as a high performer for a long time.

They might say, *"But I get results,"* or *"I'm just being honest."* They might point out that the team needs their expertise. And they may be right about some of that.

That's why I wouldn't let the conversation turn into an argument about whether they're a good employee. They can be an exceptional employee and still have behaviours that need to change, and I'd probably say so plainly:

*"You're very good at what you do. That's exactly why I'm having this conversation with you. Your contribution is valuable, but because you're influential in this team, the way you behave affects other people. I need both the performance and the behaviour."*

I think that's far more productive than pretending the performance doesn't matter. It does matter. It just isn't the only thing that does.

## The real measure of a high performer

Ultimately, I think we need a broader definition of a high performer than the person who sells the most, the engineer who closes the most tickets or whoever delivers the biggest project. Those things matter, but they're only part of the picture.

I'd much rather have someone who delivers excellent results and makes the people around them better: someone who

- shares knowledge
- challenges ideas without attacking people
- can disagree constructively
- other people want to work with
- creates more success around them, instead of making everyone else less effective.

That's the sort of high performer I'd want to build a team around.

And if someone is already delivering exceptional results but hasn't figured out the behavioural side yet, I'd want to help them develop it, not write them off. Sometimes the person with the "bad attitude" isn't a lost cause. Nobody may ever have explained clearly what their behaviour is doing to everyone else.

That's part of a manager's job too: protecting the team from difficult behaviour, helping the person understand it, giving them a chance to change, and holding them accountable if they don't. Being brilliant at your job doesn't entitle you to make everyone else's job worse, and what you tolerate today becomes the standard your team lives with tomorrow.
